title: How do you handle maps / locations?

posts.author: 3rr0r1n5ynt4x
posts.body:
Currently pondering on how I want to handle maps in the future. There 3 ways of doing this and I am unsure which one to take.
Let me show you what I mean:
This is a part of a a map I am currently working on. As you can see we have one long corridor which has 3 doors that lead into small rooms. You can walk the corridor and already see in all the other rooms. Walking to a door transfers you into that room, still on the same map, and you are free to walk around there.
Possibility 2 is to split that up, so like this:
You see no other room, when you go through a door, the corridor vanishes and you are transferred to a room:
This means you have to handle a lot more rooms but you avoid one huge map (if that is your goal). It also feels different for the player of course, but I can not really pinpoint what the different methods mean and how players react to them.
Then we have a third option, which is compromise between the 2. You have one big map but still you only show the room the player is currently active in:
I think I personally prefer this option, but what is your opinion here? When do you use one large map and when do you split the rooms? What are your feelings as player about this, in which situation to you expect which variant?

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
Your ending seems to imply you think there is a place for the different options to be present in one game - you should not do that. These are sheerly stylistic choices, and mixing styles isn't going to pan out well.
Choose which one you like best and stick with it.
The majority of JRPGs do the second one, if there are actual doors. The same majority might have something like your top map if there were no doors, just open doorways and the entire floor is one map; but I'm not sure I've ever actually seen a game do what you pictured, with doors separating spaces but it's still one map.

posts.author: utunnels
posts.body:
I have seen all 3 methods being used in games.
1. If you NEED to see the layout of the entire floor. For example an action RPG, a puzzle which you need to watch events playing next door.
2.  It is how regular people will do things.
3.  I think it is method 1 in advanced mode. Useful to create some visual effects how the player open the door and how the lighting/mask changes when they enters a room.

posts.author: alice_gristle
ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Zombie would suggest a 4th option variant, but it might be difficult to implement.
For your example, you start with just the corridor. The player isn't supposed to know what is behind a door until they go through it. But as the player explores, the map locations they visit remain visible.
So when the player enters the first room, both that room and the corridor are visible, but not the two other rooms. When the player leaves the first room, it remains visible. When the player visits the 2nd room, they now see both rooms and the corridor. And you continue.
The benefit of this is the player doesn't see what is in an area before they visit it. Which can be important for some types of games. But once the player has visited an area, their ability to see that area replicates a visual representation of their memory of that area. So it is easier if they need to return to an area.
You could even play with this a bit (again, probably difficult to implement) where the player's "memory" of areas gets fuzzy as time passes so the longer they are away from an area, the more likely it is that the area won't be visible to them when they return. Or even more difficult, there could be a possibility that the player's "memory" of an area is slightly off so what they "see" as an area they visited isn't an accurate reflection.
And if I was doing this and there were combat encounters, I would make it so the player only "recalls" the area. So anything that might wander into that area won't be visible until the player actually enters that area.
Of course, if it really doesn't matter if the player can see into areas they haven't visited yet because of they type of game you are making, then it probably doesn't matter other than design choice.
But to your original question, I think my preference would depend greatly on your type of game. But for what it is worth, if your game is good, I don't think this type of choice would effect my decision to play the game.
Good luck!

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
At one time I would have put everything of a floor of a building onto the same map. If the doors contain glass, or the party could reasonably be expected to know what was going on in the rooms before entering them, I might still do so.
Now, if the party could not reasonably be expected to know the layout and happenings of each room before exploring, the corridor and each room would be separate maps. On the other hand, I don't use as many internal doors as I used to. Oh, and unimportant areas (such as shopkeepers' living areas) would not be mapped because they are behind locked doors.
Very small maps seem to disrupt the random encounter mechanism, so, for exploring small maps I tend to use the "landmine" system. This involves using events without images that trigger a battle, and then turn themselves off, either by a self switch activating a blank event page or an "Erase Event" command. Alternatively, you can use events with the walking sprite of the enemy, but make it move faster than the player or impossible to avoid.

posts.author: Ezclados
posts.body:
As a mapper, I'm more comfortable with the second option.
If I look at the screenshots of your game, it looks like your game is not a classic RPG game, so I think you should skip the first and second options.
If your game is a horror-type or mystery-style game, I would choose the second or third option.
It all depends on what kind of theme your game has, if your game is a simulation game, I think I will use the first option.
As a player, I might prefer the third option, but there is no fadeout or transfer event, so if the player opens the door and enters the room, the room will be immediately visible, this might be difficult to implement if not using a layer plugin script. This might be suitable for action theme games

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Like most things, you need to consider "the point" of any of these styles.  But, also the map.
I did see it mentioned that "these are just styles, so pick what you like", but I don't really agree with that sentiment.  Each "style"  has its own distinct feel to a player and also serves the game mechanically.
No Transition Style
This will heavily curb exploration.  If you can already see entirely into a room, or most of the room from the hallway, and you see nothing of interest, you will bypass the room.  Players, by and large, will optimize the fun out of your game.  If a player sees an empty room with nothing to loot in it, then why go in it?  The joy of exploration and of "finding things" will diminish with this style to some degree.  Now, it is an advantage to your players as well.  It can help your players decide where to go and what to do, as well.  If they know what is in a room ahead of time, they won't have their time wasted, so you are making an anti-frustration feature.  But, then, any room that serves no purpose to gameplay exists purely as "aesthetic".  Or, rather, "to make the world feel more real".
One other issue you might have with this style is just the "the map feels too big and overwhelming".  Without enough transition points, there is no "brain reset" for the player.  A transition can be a "mental checkpoint" for a player.  It can offer some much needed "downtime", even if only 1.5 seconds for the loading of the next area.
Different Map Transitions
By and large, there's not usually a good reason to do this in an RPG Maker game, unless you have packed the map with so much stuff that it is causing actual lag in your game.  Even most SNES and Sega RPG's didn't do this.  An entire town might be on a single map.  An entire dungeon.  Just to save space.  Or, to make it easier to assign transition points to the correct maps.
Another advantage to doing this in RPG Maker is you can change tilesets between maps.  Which would allow you to have "more objects" and "more tiles" for a single location.  You could, for example, have an office with a rooftop tileset.  Or one with a pool/gym tileset.  A map transition can be to assign something "similar" to the location, but it didn't fit on the original tileset.
A disadvantage is going to be if you have rooms so close together like this... you can exhaust your player pretty quickly with how many transitions there are.  You'd have to think of so many transitions in such a short amount of time as a person who "talks so slow" in terms of exhausting.  Put simply, it will feel like this:
Same Map Transitions
I pretty much covered this under the different map transitions.
Conclusion
So, what you need to ask yourself are two questions:
1.  What am I trying to accomplish in this map in terms of gameplay and exploration?
2.  What purpose does everything in this map serve?
Number 1 will help you pick a transition style (and I don't think it's wrong to mix and match all three or more depending on what you need).  Number 2 will help you eliminate "wasted space" in your game when each part of a map needs to serve a purpose.
